limitations: GPU recommended for embedding large corpora; if LLM summarisation is enabled, outputs can hallucinate and must never be quoted without checking the source document

name: uroman
maintainer: Ulf Hermjakob, USC Information Sciences Institute
description: Universal romaniser converting text in essentially any script to the Latin alphabet without knowing the language, driven by Unicode data plus language-specific rule tables; available as a Perl script and a Python package.
journalism_use_case: Makes non-Latin-script corpora searchable and joinable — romanise Arabic, Cyrillic, Devanagari, Thai or Chinese names so a sanctions list, corporate registry and leaked ledger can be fuzzy-matched in one Latin-script index.
licence: MIT-style permissive with an added acknowledgement condition — LICENSE.txt read directly grants MIT-equivalent rights but states 'Any publication of projects using uroman shall acknowledge its use'; not a clean SPDX id (GitHub API reports NOASSERTION)
deployment: local CLI or pip library; CPU-only, negligible resources
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2024-07-26, archived=false, 257 stars; latest release v1.3.1 published 2024-06-28 — dormant since mid-2024
external_deps: none significant
data_flows: entirely local
limitations: romanisation is lossy and irreversible; output follows no single standard scheme (not ALA-LC or BGN/PCGN), so it is a matching aid rather than a citable rendering; the acknowledgement clause is a non-standard condition to track

name: VisiData
description: Terminal interface for exploring and arranging tabular data, with frequency tables, pivots, regex-driven column splitting, type detection and loaders for dozens of formats including CSV, JSON, XLSX, SQLite, PCAP and mailbox files.
journalism_use_case: First-look tool on a messy leaked dataset — profile a 10-million-row CSV, spot encoding and type breakage, and build a cleaning recipe over SSH on an air-gapped evidence machine where a GUI is not available.
deployment: local terminal app via pip or distro packages; CPU only, streams large files
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-11, archived=false, 9,473 stars
external_deps: optional per-format loader libraries (openpyxl, pandas, etc.)
data_flows: fully local
limitations: steep keyboard-driven learning curve; GPL-3.0 affects redistribution inside proprietary tooling; exploration and reshaping rather than probabilistic linkage — pair it with Splink or dedupe for matching

name: Whisper
description: Reference PyTorch implementation and weights for the Whisper encoder-decoder ASR model, covering transcription and translation across roughly 99 languages.
journalism_use_case: Baseline transcription of interviews and leaked audio where model provenance matters; the canonical implementation that nearly every newsroom transcription tool wraps.
deployment: local CLI/library; CPU or CUDA GPU
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-08-31, archived=false, 112,825 stars; upstream moves slowly while forks move faster
external_deps: PyTorch, ffmpeg; weights downloaded on first run
data_flows: fully local inference after weight download; no audio leaves the machine
limitations: no speaker diarisation; approximate word timestamps; large-v3 needs roughly 10GB VRAM; prone to hallucinated text on silence and poor recordings

name: whisper.cpp
description: Plain C/C++ port of Whisper inference on the ggml tensor library, with quantised models, CoreML/Metal/CUDA/Vulkan backends, and a bundled CLI and server.
journalism_use_case: Transcribing suspect audio and video locally so the words in a claimed 'leaked recording' can be checked, searched and quoted without uploading sensitive source material to any transcription service. Transcripts also feed quote-matching against known speeches to spot recycled or spliced audio.
deployment: local binary/library; CPU, Apple Silicon Metal/CoreML, CUDA, Vulkan; mobile and embedded targets
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-16, archived=false, 55,238 stars; release v1.9.5 published 2026-10-06
external_deps: ffmpeg for format conversion; optional backend SDKs
data_flows: fully local; model files fetched once
limitations: no built-in diarisation; quantisation trades accuracy for speed; API churn across releases can break downstream wrappers

name: WhisperX
description: Pipeline combining faster-whisper transcription with wav2vec2 forced alignment for accurate word-level timestamps and optional pyannote speaker diarisation.
journalism_use_case: Producing quote-accurate, speaker-attributed transcripts of multi-party interviews and hearings, where you must jump to the exact second a phrase was spoken to verify it.
model_licence: mixed — Whisper MIT; wav2vec2 aligners vary by language; pyannote diarisation weights MIT but gated on HuggingFace
deployment: local CLI and Python API; CUDA GPU strongly preferred
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-12, archived=false, 25,364 stars; release v3.8.6 published 2026-05-25
external_deps: faster-whisper, pyannote.audio, torchaudio, ffmpeg; HuggingFace token for gated diarisation models
data_flows: local inference, but obtaining diarisation weights requires accepting pyannote's HuggingFace gate, which discloses your HF identity to the model authors
limitations: diarisation degrades on overlapping speech and phone audio; alignment-model coverage is uneven outside major languages; heavy dependency stack; ~10GB VRAM for large-v3 plus diarisation

name: yente
description: Self-hostable HTTP API for entity search and bulk matching against sanctions, PEP and other FollowTheMoney collections, backed by Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and implementing the Reconciliation Service API so OpenRefine can point at it directly.
journalism_use_case: Screen a leaked client or shareholder list against sanctions and PEP data in bulk on your own infrastructure, then reconcile the same spreadsheet from OpenRefine without the names leaving your network.
deployment: Docker Compose with Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, fully self-hosted; CPU only, moderate RAM for the index
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: pushed_at 2026-11-16, archived=false, 184 stars; release v5.5.1 published 2026-10-30
external_deps: Elasticsearch or OpenSearch; OpenSanctions bulk data files loaded at index time
data_flows: queries stay local once indexed — the key privacy win over hosted screening APIs. The index DATA is licensed separately by OpenSanctions (CC-BY-NC with paid commercial tiers)
limitations: code is MIT but the data it exists to serve is non-commercial unless licensed, which directly affects commercial newsrooms; matching returns scored candidates that still need human adjudication; the index must be refreshed to stay current

name: AASIST
description: Official PyTorch implementation of 'AASIST: Audio Anti-Spoofing using Integrated Spectro-Temporal Graph Attention Networks', an end-to-end raw-waveform spoofing countermeasure. Two pretrained models included: AASIST (reported EER 0.83%, min t-DCF 0.0275) and lightweight AASIST-L (EER 0.99%, min t-DCF 0.0309, 85,306 parameters).
journalism_use_case: Screening suspect voice notes, leaked 'audio recordings' of politicians and robocall clips for synthesis or voice-conversion artefacts - the audio half of verification, where there is far less tooling than for video.
model_licence: MIT (pretrained models shipped in-repo under the same licence)
deployment: self-hosted; ~16GB VRAM cited for training at batch size 24, inference far lighter
activity_evidence: Repo page shows only 5 commits on main and a NAVER copyright of '2021-present'; not marked archived but essentially frozen research code
external_deps: ASVspoof 2019 LA dataset for training/evaluation (separate terms)
data_flows: Fully local inference; no API keys
limitations: Outputs a probabilistic spoofing score, NOT proof that audio is synthetic. The headline sub-1% EER figures are on ASVspoof 2019 logical access - a clean, studio-condition benchmark. Published in-the-wild evaluations show audio detector AUC collapsing on real circulated media; telephony codecs, compression, background noise, short clips and post-2019 generators are all unaddressed. Repo is effectively unmaintained.

name: Alegre (Meedan Check)
description: Media and text similarity analysis service underpinning Check: a Flask service exposing similarity search and classification over images, video, audio and text (including language detection and translation-memory style matching), backed by Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and PostgreSQL.
journalism_use_case: Powers tipline and fact-check deduplication at scale - when a reader submits an image or claim, Alegre finds whether a near-identical item has already been received and checked, so the desk answers from existing work instead of re-verifying.
model_licence: varies - bundles third-party sentence-transformer/BERT checkpoints whose own licences were not verified
deployment: self-hosted via docker-compose (API with Swagger UI on :3100)
activity_evidence: Commit feed on develop: 2026-09-28 merge of PR #513, 2026-09-27 Dockerfile production fixes, 2026-06-01 PR #512; 784 commits, 21 open PRs
external_deps: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, PostgreSQL, Docker; ML model downloads; Google Translate API optional
data_flows: Self-hostable so media and hashes can stay on infrastructure you control; optional translation/LLM integrations send text to third parties - audit configuration before handling sensitive material
limitations: Similarity matching answers 'have we seen this before?', not 'is this real?' - outputs are probabilistic similarity signals, not conclusive proof of manipulation or reuse. No synthetic-media detection. Operationally heavy. Thresholds must be tuned per language and media type to avoid merging genuinely different items.

name: ASVspoof 2021 baseline systems
description: Baseline countermeasure systems and official evaluation tooling for the ASVspoof 2021 challenge across its LA, PA and DF tracks. Includes CQCC-GMM and LFCC-GMM (MATLAB and Python), LFCC-LCNN and RawNet2 (PyTorch), plus min t-DCF / EER scoring tools, full key sets, meta-labels and an interactive evaluation notebook.
journalism_use_case: The reference implementations and, more importantly, the official scoring code for audio deepfake detection - what you use to independently compute EER on your own test clips rather than accepting a vendor's self-reported number.
deployment: self-hosted
activity_evidence: Repo page shows 13 commits on main, 259 stars, 90 forks, 14 open issues; the 2021 challenge is concluded and the repo serves as its archive of baselines and keys
external_deps: MATLAB required for the GMM baselines' original versions (Python ports provided); ASVspoof evaluation data obtained separately
data_flows: Local training, inference and scoring; no third-party API calls
limitations: No root LICENSE file was found (a fetch of /blob/main/LICENSE returned 404), so licensing could not be confirmed and may differ per baseline subdirectory - treat reuse as legally unresolved. Technically these are 2021-era simple reference systems, not state of the art, and the DF track data predates current TTS and voice-cloning models. Scores are probabilistic signals, not conclusive proof.

name: AVeriTeC dataset and baseline
maintainer: Michael Schlichtkrull et al., University of Cambridge
description: Dataset and multi-stage baseline for verifying 4,500+ real claims drawn from fact-checks by ~50 organisations. Each claim is annotated with question-answer evidence pairs and a textual justification; the baseline runs coarse web retrieval, question generation, reranking, veracity prediction and justification generation.
journalism_use_case: The closest public benchmark to actual fact-checking practice: it models verification as asking and answering questions against open web evidence and producing a written justification, mirroring how a fact-checker works.
deployment: local research pipeline
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: 84 stars, last push 2024-11-27, archived=false. Dormant ~2 years.
external_deps: Google Programmable Search API key and CSE ID REQUIRED for coarse retrieval; large local disk; LLM for question generation
data_flows: Claim text and generated queries are sent to Google's Search API; retrieved pages cached locally. Depending on model choice, text may also go to a third-party LLM provider.
limitations: Licence could NOT be confirmed: no LICENSE/COPYING file in the repo root, GitHub API reports no detected licence, README has no licence section - redistribution and commercial terms unknown. Verdicts are probabilistic, not proof. Results sensitive to search-API recall and to evidence published after the claim date (temporal leakage).

name: CAT-Net (Compression Artifact Tracing Network)
description: Official implementation of CAT-Net v1 (WACV 2021, splicing-only) and v2 (IJCV 2022, general forgery), localising manipulated regions by tracing inconsistencies in JPEG compression artifacts, combining an RGB stream with a DCT/quantisation-table stream.
journalism_use_case: Spotting spliced-in regions in JPEGs that still retain their original compression history - for example a photo circulated as a camera original rather than a platform re-encode.
model_licence: CC-BY-4.0 (pretrained weights and released datasets), per the README licence section
deployment: local training/inference scripts; weights downloaded manually
activity_evidence: Commit feed: 2026-10-15 merge of PR #57, 2026-10-09 fix for quantisation-table dtype under NumPy 1.24+, 2026-08-05 README commits relaxing licence terms; 316 stars
external_deps: PyTorch; pretrained and trained weights hosted on Google Drive and Baiduyun
data_flows: Weights pulled from third-party file hosts (Google Drive / Baiduyun); inference is local
limitations: Depends on JPEG compression artifacts, so its signal is weak or absent for PNG/screenshot/heavily re-encoded images - exactly the state most social-media images arrive in. v1 handles splicing only. Localisation maps are probabilistic indications, NOT conclusive proof of manipulation. README warns users remain responsible for the copyright status of images in referenced datasets.

name: ClaimBuster-Spotter
maintainer: IDIR Lab, University of Texas at Arlington
description: Reference implementations of ClaimBuster check-worthiness scoring: SVM, bidirectional LSTM, and adversarial-training-on-transformers models that score sentences for how check-worthy a factual claim they contain. Colab notebooks accompany each variant.
journalism_use_case: Automatically rank sentences from debate transcripts, speeches or long interviews by check-worthiness so a fact-checking desk can prioritise which statements to verify under deadline.
model_licence: not verified - trained checkpoints not clearly licensed in-repo; the hosted ClaimBuster API has its own terms
deployment: local training/inference; Colab notebooks; separate hosted ClaimBuster API exists
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: 87 stars, 26 open issues, last push 2023-11-29, archived=false but dormant ~3 years.
external_deps: TensorFlow, pretrained transformer checkpoints; ClaimBuster datasets requested separately
data_flows: runs locally - no third-party calls for models in this repo. Using claimbuster.org's hosted API instead sends your text to UT Arlington.
limitations: Check-worthiness scores are probabilistic prioritisation signals, not judgements of truth and not conclusive proof of anything - a high score means 'worth checking', not 'false'. Trained predominantly on US political-debate English. Dormant codebase on older TensorFlow. GPL-3.0 copyleft constrains embedding in proprietary tools.

name: ClaimsKG extractor
description: Web-scraping component of ClaimsKG. Crawls a curated list of IFCN-signatory fact-checking sites and emits a CSV dump of extracted claims, ratings and metadata, which claimskg_generator lifts into an RDF knowledge graph.
journalism_use_case: Build a cross-organisation database of already-published fact-checks (Full Fact, Snopes, PolitiFact, Africa Check, AFP Fact Check, EUvsDisinfo) to check whether a circulating claim has already been debunked.
deployment: local CLI; outputs CSV for the RDF generator
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: 21 stars, last push 2022-09-01, archived=false but dormant ~4 years. Siblings also dormant: claimskg_generator 2022-09-02, claimskg-embeddings 2023-03-31.
external_deps: live fact-checking websites (scraped); optional entity linking via TagMe in the wider pipeline
data_flows: scrapes third-party fact-checker websites directly; your crawling traffic is visible to those sites. No credentials required.
limitations: Licence could NOT be confirmed: GitHub licence API returns 404 and no LICENSE file is detected; the code is also a fork of vwoloszyn/fake_news_extractor, compounding provenance uncertainty. Only English extractors stated functional. Site-specific scrapers break as fact-checkers redesign; after ~4 years dormant many are likely broken.

name: Community Forensics
description: Training and evaluation pipeline plus released detectors for the CVPR 2025 paper 'Community Forensics: Using Thousands of Generators to Train Fake Image Detectors'. Dataset spans 4,803 generative models and ~2.7M images. Checkpoints published at 224px and 384px input sizes (21.8M parameters, Safetensors).
journalism_use_case: The most defensible currently-available open detector baseline for 'is this image synthetic?' triage, because its training distribution covers thousands of generators rather than a handful - still a lead generator, not an adjudicator.
model_licence: MIT (stated on the OwensLab/commfor-model-384 Hugging Face model card)
language_stack: Python, PyTorch (torchrun distributed), Hugging Face Hub
deployment: local training/inference after downloading weights; datasets very large (Small 278GB, full 1.1TB)
activity_evidence: Commit feed: 2025-10-18 README/eval-set updates and HF test-repo split renames, 2025-08-29 and 2025-08-28 README commits; 11 commits on main; HF card reports ~3,263 downloads in the last month
external_deps: Hugging Face Hub (model and dataset repos), Dropbox-hosted PyTorch checkpoints, PyTorch
data_flows: Weights and datasets fetched from Hugging Face and Dropbox; after download, inference runs locally so case images need not be uploaded
limitations: Output is a probability, i.e. an assistive signal - it cannot establish that an image was or was not AI-generated and is not conclusive proof. The repository does not document accuracy bounds, calibration or generalisation limits, so a newsroom cannot cite an error rate from it; published numbers come from benchmark conditions, not platform-degraded images. Needs GPU capacity and terabyte-scale storage.

name: CooRnet
description: R package that, given a set of URLs, detected coordinated link-sharing behaviour on Facebook and Instagram and output the network of entities performing it. The original and widely-cited implementation of the coordinated-link-sharing method.
journalism_use_case: Historically the standard tool for showing a false claim was amplified by a coordinated page network; now relevant mainly for reproducing or auditing past published investigations.
deployment: local R package (non-functional without CrowdTangle)
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: archived=true, 75 stars, last push 2024-08-14. README states CrowdTangle is no longer available as of 2024-08-14 and points users to CooRTweet and coordination-network-toolkit.
external_deps: CrowdTangle API key - service shut down 2024-08-14, so the data layer no longer exists
data_flows: historically sent URL lists to Meta's CrowdTangle API; now inoperable
limitations: Archived and functionally dead: its only data source was discontinued. Use the maintainer's named successors. Kept for reference implementation value and methodological citation.

name: CooRTweet
description: R package that detects coordinated behaviour on social media - co-sharing of links, co-retweets, co-hashtags, near-identical text within a time window - and outputs the network of coordinated accounts with supporting statistics. Maintained successor recommended by the archived CooRnet.
journalism_use_case: Investigating whether a claim's apparent virality is organic or amplified: identify clusters of accounts pushing the same content in lockstep, a standard evidentiary step in disinformation-campaign reporting.
deployment: local R package, install from CRAN or GitHub
activity_evidence: Verified 2026-11-16: 57 stars, archived=false, last push 2026-11-08. DESCRIPTION shows Version 2.2.0, Date 2026-10-22, 'License: MIT + file LICENSE'. GitHub reports NOASSERTION because LICENSE is the R-convention stub, so DESCRIPTION was read to confirm MIT.
external_deps: R and standard data/network packages; you must supply the social-media data yourself
data_flows: analysis is fully local on data you already hold - the package does not call platform APIs. Obtaining input data requires platform API access subject to those platforms' terms.
limitations: Detects statistical co-occurrence, not intent - outputs are probabilistic signals, not proof of a coordinated campaign; a cluster may be a campaign, a fan community, a newsletter, or an artefact of the chosen time window. Highly sensitive to time-window and minimum-participation parameters, which must be stated with any finding. Requires researcher-level platform data access, much harder since CrowdTangle's shutdown.

name: Deepfake-Eval-2024
description: Multi-modal in-the-wild deepfake benchmark of media actually circulated in 2024, collected from social media and the TrueMedia.org detection platform: 44 hours of video, 56.5 hours of audio and 1,975 images spanning 88 website sources and 52 languages. The GitHub repo is primarily documentation and labelling examples; the dataset is hosted on Hugging Face.
journalism_use_case: The citation to reach for when an editor or vendor claims a detector is '98% accurate'. Its central finding is that open-source state-of-the-art detector AUC drops by roughly 50% for video, 48% for audio and 45% for image models when moved from academic benchmarks to real circulated deepfakes - the single most useful calibration fact for newsroom policy on detector outputs.
model_licence: not verified - dataset distributed via Hugging Face under terms not confirmed at the repo page
language_stack: documentation/data (no training code observed in repo)
deployment: dataset download + own evaluation harness
activity_evidence: Repo page shows 11 commits on main, 17 stars, 1 fork, 1 open issue; associated paper arXiv 2503.02857 (2025); not archived
external_deps: Dataset hosted on Hugging Face, separate from the GitHub repo
data_flows: Dataset retrieval from Hugging Face; no runtime service
limitations: No licence for code or data was visible on the repo page, so redistribution and commercial use are legally unresolved. The repo contains no fine-tuning or evaluation code, only documentation and labelling examples. The accuracy-drop figures come from the paper rather than the repo, and as a 2024 snapshot it will itself date as generators change. It is a measuring stick, not a detector - it produces no authenticity judgements at all.

name: DeepfakeBench
description: Unified benchmark and training/evaluation framework for deepfake detection with standardised data management and evaluation protocols. Repo lists 36 detectors (5 naive, 20 spatial, 3 frequency, 8 video-based, including Effort from ICML 2025) across 9 datasets including FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF v1/v2, UADFV and DFDC variants, with pre-trained weights on the releases page.
journalism_use_case: The practical way a technically-staffed newsroom or research partner can run several published face-manipulation detectors over the same suspect video and see whether they agree, instead of trusting one black-box score. Also the reference for telling an editor how a detector actually performed on benchmark data versus vendor claims.
model_licence: CC-BY-NC-4.0 for the framework; per-dataset terms vary and the repo marks some datasets as not rights-cleared
deployment: self-hosted, GPU required
activity_evidence: Repo page shows 218 commits on main, v1.0.1+ releases carrying pre-trained weights, and inclusion of a 2025 method (Effort, ICML 2025 Spotlight); not archived
external_deps: PyTorch/CUDA; benchmark datasets obtained separately under their own agreements
data_flows: Local training and inference; dataset acquisition involves third-party request forms and downloads
limitations: Outputs are probabilistic scores, NEVER conclusive proof of manipulation. The project's own framing is that cross-dataset generalisation remains the open problem: detectors scoring near-perfectly in-dataset degrade substantially on unseen generators, recompressed uploads and out-of-distribution faces. Non-commercial licence excludes commercial newsroom use without separate permission; several bundled datasets are explicitly not rights-cleared.

name: DEFAME
description: Dynamic Evidence-based Fact-checking with Multimodal Experts: an agentic fact-checking system handling text and image inputs, planning and invoking tools (web search, reverse image search, geolocation, OCR, image forensics) to gather evidence and produce a verdict with written justification.
journalism_use_case: Verification of image-plus-text claims as they actually circulate on social media - where the claim is a photo with a caption - producing a tool-by-tool evidence trail a journalist can audit rather than a bare label.
model_licence: n/a by default - uses hosted LLMs (default GPT-4o); optional local GPU components pull third-party models whose licences were not verified
language_stack: Python; Docker images at tudamailab/defame; optional CUDA
deployment: Docker Compose or manual pip install; prompts for API keys on first run
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: 62 stars, Apache-2.0, archived=false, repo last push 2026-05-21 but last commit on default branch 2025-09-30. ICML paper arXiv 2412.10510.
external_deps: API keys for an LLM (GPT-4o default) and for search/reverse-image tools; Docker; optional CUDA GPU
data_flows: NOT local by default. Claim text and submitted images are sent to the configured LLM provider and to external search/reverse-image services. Running it on unpublished source imagery exposes that imagery to third parties.
limitations: Research prototype - verdicts and the evidence chain are probabilistic model output requiring human adjudication, never proof. Image forensics and geolocation outputs are leads, not determinations. High cost and latency per claim. Default branch static since Sept 2025.

name: ExifTool
description: Reference command-line tool and Perl library for reading, writing and creating metadata across a very wide range of formats and standards - EXIF, GPS, IPTC, XMP, MakerNotes from Canon/Nikon/Sony and others, Photoshop IRB, ICC profiles, JFIF, PDF, PNG, MIE, and C2PA among writable types.
journalism_use_case: First step on almost every image verification: dump the full metadata block to read capture time, GPS coordinates, device and lens, software history and embedded thumbnails (an embedded thumbnail disagreeing with the main image is a classic editing tell).
deployment: local CLI / Perl library; packaged for Windows, macOS and Linux
activity_evidence: Commit feed shows version bumps 13.63 on 2026-11-10, 13.62 on 2026-11-09, 13.61 on 2026-11-05 and 13.60 on 2026-10-28 - very regular release cadence
external_deps: none beyond Perl for core use
data_flows: Entirely local; nothing transmitted, which makes it safe for source-sensitive material
limitations: Metadata is evidence about a file, not about reality: every field can also be written or stripped (by ExifTool itself), so a plausible EXIF block is not authentication and never conclusive proof. Most social platforms strip metadata on upload, so an empty block is the normal case and proves nothing. GPS tags may be absent, imprecise or deliberately falsified.

name: FaceForensics++
maintainer: Andreas Roessler et al., TU Munich
description: Forensics dataset and baseline code: 1,000 original video sequences manipulated by Deepfakes, Face2Face, FaceSwap, NeuralTextures and later FaceShifter, sourced from 977 YouTube videos. Includes binary masks, 1,000 deepfake generation models, the Google/Jigsaw Deep Fake Detection Dataset (3,000+ videos), classification samples and a hidden-set benchmark.
journalism_use_case: The canonical reference corpus behind most published face-swap detectors - useful to a newsroom's technical partner for sanity-checking any vendor-pitched detector, and to reporters as the citation for why detector accuracy figures in press releases are usually in-dataset numbers.
model_licence: Data released under the separate 'FaceForensics Terms of Use' (research-oriented PDF agreement) - not an SPDX open licence
deployment: self-hosted; dataset gated
activity_evidence: Repo page shows 61 commits on master, 2.8k stars, 84 open issues; last substantive feature noted is the FaceShifter addition dated 2020-07-15
external_deps: Access requires completing a Google Form; approved applicants receive a download script link
data_flows: Dataset request flows through a Google Form and the authors' email; download script pulls from the project's servers
limitations: Dated relative to current generators - predates modern diffusion and audio-driven video synthesis, so a detector trained only on FF++ transfers poorly to 2024-2026 in-the-wild fakes; any detector score built on it is a probabilistic signal, not proof. Code is MIT but the data is not open: Terms of Use are a separate agreement gating redistribution and commercial use. Maintenance effectively dormant since 2020.

name: FacTool
description: Task- and domain-agnostic framework for detecting factual errors in generated text. Extracts atomic claims, generates queries, collects evidence, and reasons to a per-claim factuality judgement across knowledge-based QA, code, math and scientific-literature settings.
journalism_use_case: Auditing AI-generated or AI-assisted copy before publication, and as a reusable claim-extraction-plus-evidence-collection component inside a newsroom verification pipeline.
deployment: pip-installable library / local scripts calling remote APIs
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: 937 stars, Apache-2.0, archived=false, last push and last commit 2024-08-19 - dormant ~2 years.
external_deps: OpenAI API key and a search API (Serper/Google) for the knowledge-QA scenario
data_flows: NOT local - submitted text, extracted claims and generated search queries go to the configured LLM provider and search API.
limitations: Outputs are probabilistic factuality signals for triage, not conclusive verification or proof; the paper frames it as error detection in generated text rather than adjudication of public claims. Dormant since Aug 2024 so pinned model names may have drifted. Evidence quality bounded by the search backend.

name: Fetch (Meedan ClaimReview aggregator)
description: Service that aggregated fact-checks from multiple publisher sources and re-exposed them as schema.org ClaimReview records for consumption by the Check platform.
journalism_use_case: Reference implementation for normalising heterogeneous fact-check feeds into ClaimReview so a newsroom can query across many fact-checking organisations' outputs from one index.
deployment: self-hosted service (historically)
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: archived=true, 1 star, last push 2026-05-21.
external_deps: source-specific fact-check feed endpoints/APIs
data_flows: fetches from third-party fact-checker sites/APIs; outputs ClaimReview JSON
limitations: Archived and unmaintained - feed adapters for third-party sites rot quickly. Reference only for ClaimReview normalisation patterns.

name: FEVER platform and baselines
description: FEVER annotation platform plus baseline systems for the canonical claim-verification benchmark: given a claim, retrieve Wikipedia evidence sentences and classify SUPPORTED / REFUTED / NOT ENOUGH INFO.
journalism_use_case: Standard reference point for evaluating any evidence-retrieval-plus-entailment pipeline before trusting it on real claims; the annotation platform is reusable for building a newsroom's own claim/evidence gold set.
model_licence: not verified - baseline checkpoints downloaded separately; Wikipedia evidence corpus is CC-BY-SA
deployment: self-hosted / local research use
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: 130 stars, Apache-2.0, last push 2026-02-20, archived=false. Older baseline repo sheffieldnlp/naacl2018-fever IS archived (last push 2023-02-03).
external_deps: FEVER dataset and Wikipedia dump downloads; Python ML stack
data_flows: fully local once data is downloaded; no third-party API keys required
limitations: Claims are human-written over Wikipedia, not real-world political or social-media claims, so FEVER scores systematically overstate real-world performance. Verdicts are probabilistic classifications, not adjudications or proof. Baseline code is research-grade.

name: Full Fact AI Trust Benchmark
description: Public repository sharing code and data from Full Fact's AI Trust Benchmark - a fact-checking organisation's own framework for measuring how trustworthy AI systems are when handling factual and misinformation-adjacent queries.
journalism_use_case: Gives a newsroom a practitioner-authored, rather than vendor-authored, basis for deciding whether an AI assistant is fit to be placed near editorial fact-checking work.
model_licence: n/a - evaluates third-party models, distributes none
deployment: local evaluation scripts against model APIs
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: 3 stars, Apache-2.0, archived=false, last push 2026-11-03 - currently active. Org also has FullFact/health-misinfo-shared (MIT, last push 2025-08-14).
external_deps: API access to whichever models are being benchmarked
data_flows: benchmark prompts are sent to the model providers under evaluation
limitations: Very low adoption signal (3 stars) and early-stage; a benchmark rather than a fact-checking tool. Scores are probabilistic snapshots of specific model versions and go stale quickly. Full Fact's production automated-fact-checking stack is NOT open-sourced - do not expect a deployable Full Fact pipeline here.

name: GeoCLIP
description: CLIP-inspired model for worldwide image geo-localisation that contrastively aligns image embeddings with GPS coordinate embeddings, trained on ~4.7M geo-tagged images; ships a reusable pretrained LocationEncoder and reports state-of-the-art results on Im2GPS3k, YFCC26k, GWS15k and Geo-Tagged NUS-Wide.
journalism_use_case: Narrowing the search space when geolocating a photo with no metadata: GeoCLIP proposes candidate regions, which an investigator then confirms or rejects by matching buildings, signage, vegetation and terrain against satellite and street-level imagery.
model_licence: not separately stated; pretrained weights distributed with the MIT-licensed package
deployment: pip install geoclip; local inference
activity_evidence: Commit feed: 2026-10-25 'Update Pillow and Python requirements', 2026-10-07 release 1.2.3 plus untrained-CLIP initialisation option, 2026-10-06 release 1.2.2; 46 commits on main, 419 stars
external_deps: PyTorch, CLIP backbone, pretrained weights download
data_flows: Inference is local once installed, so case images need not be sent to a geolocation API
limitations: Produces a probabilistic guess over coordinates, NEVER a location fact or proof - benchmark accuracy says nothing about any individual image and the README states no per-image accuracy figures. Biased toward places well represented in geo-tagged training data (tourist-heavy, Global North) and degrades on indoor, close-up, night-time and visually generic scenes. Never publish a GeoCLIP output as a located claim without independent visual confirmation.

name: Google Fact Check Tools API
description: Two hosted APIs: a Claim Search API querying the corpus of published ClaimReview fact-checks surfaced in Fact Check Explorer, and a ClaimReview read/write API letting a verified site owner add, edit or delete ClaimReview markup for their fact-check articles.
journalism_use_case: Check whether a circulating claim has already been fact-checked by any publisher worldwide before spending desk time on it, and publish your own fact-checks as structured ClaimReview so they are discoverable by others.
deployment: hosted Google service only - no self-hosting, no source code
activity_evidence: Documentation live and fetched 2026-11-16. No public repository so no commit/release history. Third-party OSS clients exist (e.g. MartinoMensio/claimreview-collector, last push 2026-11-09) of varying licence quality.
external_deps: Google API key for Claim Search; Google Search Console verification for the ClaimReview write API
data_flows: Queries and submitted ClaimReview markup go to Google. Documentation states API users must inform their own users that the API contributes data to Data Commons - submitted fact-check data is redistributed onward.
limitations: NOT open source: hosted service under Google's API Terms, with deprecation and quota risk outside your control. Coverage is limited to publishers emitting valid ClaimReview markup, skewing toward larger English-language fact-checkers; absence of a result is not evidence a claim is unchecked. Listed because it anchors the ClaimReview ecosystem several OSS tools depend on.

name: ImageHash
description: Python perceptual-hashing library implementing average hash, perceptual hash (DCT-based), difference hash, wavelet hash, HSV colour hash and a crop-resistant hash, with adjustable hash size; hashes serialise to hex and compare by Hamming distance.
journalism_use_case: Build an in-house index of images you have already seen or debunked, then test whether a newly circulating image is a re-post, a crop or a lightly edited variant - the local alternative to pasting a sensitive image into a commercial reverse-image-search service.
deployment: local Python library (PyPI)
activity_evidence: Commit feed: 2026-10-12 pycodestyle lint target, 2026-10-05 merge of PR #231 skipping empty crops in crop-resistant hashing, 2026-09-26 merge of PR #230; 358 commits, 3.9k stars, GitHub Actions CI
external_deps: Pillow, NumPy, SciPy
data_flows: Local only; no external service required
limitations: A hash match is a probabilistic similarity signal, not provenance and not proof - it tells you two files look alike, not which came first or whether either is authentic. Classic perceptual hashes degrade under cropping, rotation, overlaid captions and heavy re-encoding (the crop-resistant variant only partly mitigates), and false positives on flat images are a known failure mode. Threshold tuning is the analyst's responsibility.

name: InVID-WeVerify Verification Plugin
maintainer: AFP Medialab (InVID / WeVerify / vera.ai EU projects)
description: Browser-extension verification toolkit: splits social video into keyframes, runs reverse image search across Google/Baidu/Yandex, reads image and video metadata, applies forensic filters, offers magnifier, image enhancement, advanced social search and synthetic-media detection panels.
journalism_use_case: Front-line triage of a viral image or video claim: establish whether media is recycled, find earliest appearance, inspect EXIF, and gather forensic and synthetic-media signals before publishing a verification.
model_licence: n/a for the extension code - deepfake/forensics models run on AFP/vera.ai backend services; weights not distributed and model licences not verified
language_stack: JavaScript / React browser extension (Chrome and Firefox)
deployment: browser extension; analysis features call AFP-hosted backend APIs
external_deps: AFP/vera.ai backend microservices; third-party reverse-image engines (Google, Baidu, Yandex); Matomo analytics
data_flows: NOT local-only. Media submitted for keyframes, forensics, deepfake detection, translation or archiving is uploaded to AFP/vera.ai backends; reverse-image search sends images or URLs to Google/Baidu/Yandex; Matomo collects usage telemetry.
limitations: Forensic and AI/deepfake panel outputs are probabilistic signals and investigative leads, NOT conclusive proof of manipulation or synthesis - false positives and negatives occur and platform recompression degrades forensic signals. No explicit probabilistic-output disclaimer found in the repo README. Depends on AFP-hosted backends remaining available.

name: kuroi
description: ICIJ tool for LLM-assisted stripping of sensitive data from PDFs - identifying and removing personal or identifying information before documents are shared or published.
journalism_use_case: The publishing-side counterpart to x-ray: before an investigative team releases primary-source documents, use it to find and remove source-identifying and personal data at scale rather than redacting page by page.
model_licence: n/a - depends on whichever LLM the operator configures
deployment: self-hosted CLI; LLM backend operator-configured
activity_evidence: gh api 2026-11-16: AGPL-3.0, archived=false, last push 2026-10-13, 6 stars - very new and low adoption
external_deps: An LLM backend (local or hosted) for sensitive-entity identification
data_flows: CRITICAL: if configured against a hosted LLM, the sensitive document content being redacted is sent to that provider - the exact opposite of the tool's purpose. Use a local model for genuinely sensitive material.
limitations: LLM-based detection of sensitive data is probabilistic, NOT conclusive - it will miss identifiers and flag non-sensitive text, so output must be human-reviewed before any release. Very low adoption (6 stars) and recent, so maturity is unproven. AGPL-3.0 copyleft. Never treat an automated pass as sufficient redaction for source protection.

name: LAA-Net
maintainer: Nguyen et al., SnT / University of Luxembourg
description: Official implementation of the CVPR 2024 paper 'LAA-Net: Localized Artifact Attention Network for Quality-Agnostic and Generalizable Deepfake Detection'. Combines heatmap-based and self-consistency attention in a multi-task setup with an Enhanced Feature Pyramid Network to focus on small artifact-prone facial regions.
journalism_use_case: A quality-agnostic detector aimed at the verification pain point most detectors fail on - compressed social-media re-uploads; relevant as a second or third opinion in a technical partner's detector ensemble, not as a standalone verdict tool.
model_licence: SnT Academic License - README states the software is copyright University of Luxembourg and licensed under the SnT academic licence (academic use only, not OSI-approved)
deployment: self-hosted, GPU
activity_evidence: Repo page shows 13 commits on main, 180 stars, 19 open issues, last substantive update around 2024-02-26; not archived but quiet
external_deps: Facial alignment and landmark detection preprocessing; pinned older CUDA/PyTorch versions
data_flows: Local inference; benchmark datasets obtained separately under their own terms
limitations: Academic licence means it is not usable as commercial newsroom infrastructure without permission. Outputs are probabilistic signals, not conclusive proof of manipulation. Reported numbers show the familiar in-dataset/cross-dataset gap: ~99.95% AUC on FF++ in-dataset versus ~86.3% on Celeb-DF and ~86.9% on DFDC. Pinned legacy CUDA/PyTorch and heavy preprocessing make setup brittle; near-dormant since early 2024.

name: Loki (OpenFactVerification)
description: End-to-end factuality pipeline that decomposes a document into atomic claims, filters for check-worthiness, retrieves web evidence and produces a per-claim verdict. Ships a CLI, Python library interface and web demo app.
journalism_use_case: First-pass screening of a long text - press release, transcript, filed story or AI-generated draft - into a ranked list of discrete checkable claims with candidate evidence links, which a journalist then verifies manually.
model_licence: n/a - calls hosted LLM APIs rather than bundling weights
deployment: pip/local CLI, Python library, or local web app; depends on remote LLM and search APIs
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: 1,164 stars, MIT, archived=false, but last push and last commit both 2024-10-03 - unmaintained ~2 years despite high star count.
external_deps: OPENAI_API_KEY required for all tasks per README; SERPER_API_KEY required for evidence retrieval with the Serper backend
data_flows: NOT local. Submitted text and generated claims/queries are sent to OpenAI and Serper (Google Search proxy). Unsuitable for unpublished or source-sensitive material without replacing both backends.
limitations: Verdicts are LLM-generated probabilistic assessments with known failure modes (hallucinated reasoning, over-trust in low-quality retrieved sources, prompt and search-ranking sensitivity) - assistance, not proof. No accuracy figures verified at the repo. Dormant since late 2024 so API/model drift is likely. Per-document API costs scale with claim count.

name: mat2 (Metadata Anonymisation Toolkit 2)
description: Metadata scrubber providing the libmat2 Python library, a mat2 CLI and file-manager integrations. Handles 20+ format families including JPEG, PNG, TIFF, WebP, AVIF, JXL, GIF, BMP, SVG, PDF, DOCX/XLSX/PPTX, EPUB, audio/video containers and archives.
journalism_use_case: The counterpart to verification: strip identifying metadata from images before publishing or sharing them, so a published photo does not burn the source's device, location or filesystem trail.
language_stack: Python (with GdkPixbuf/Cairo/Poppler-class bindings for some formats)
deployment: local CLI, Python library, file-manager extensions; packaged widely by Linux distributions
activity_evidence: Commit feed: 2026-11-15 'Accept the mp4 movie timescale written by ffmpeg 9', 2026-11-10 unreadable-file error message, 2026-10-08 packaging commits; PyPI shows version 0.15.0 released 2026-08-04; 703 commits on main
external_deps: per-format system libraries; --check-dependencies reports what is available
data_flows: Fully local processing - nothing uploaded, which is the point for source-protection work
limitations: Cleaning is best-effort and format-specific: unsupported formats may be refused or incompletely cleaned, and mat2 cannot remove information in visible pixels (reflections, screen contents, identifiable surroundings) or content-level identifiers. Verify output with ExifTool before publishing. Canonical upstream repo is 0xacab.org/jvoisin/mat2, which blocked automated fetching; GitHub mirror and PyPI used as verified sources.

name: MediaInfo
description: Cross-platform CLI, GUI and library reporting technical and tag data for video and audio files: container and codec identity, encoder strings, bitrate, frame rate, resolution, stream order, duration and embedded tags. Ships Qt/wxWidgets/VCL/UWP front-ends plus Android and iOS builds.
journalism_use_case: Establish provenance signals on a submitted video before content analysis: which app or device wrote the file, whether the container layout matches a direct camera export or a WhatsApp/Telegram re-encode, and whether two 'different' files share an identical encoder signature.
deployment: local desktop app / CLI / embeddable library
activity_evidence: Repo page shows 2,937 commits on master and current build instructions for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS; not archived. A specific latest-release date was not captured.
external_deps: MediaInfoLib; GUI toolkit of choice at build time
data_flows: Entirely local file inspection; no network dependency
limitations: Reports only what the file declares. Metadata is trivially stripped or forged and almost every social platform re-encodes on upload, destroying original encoder fields - absence of suspicious metadata is not evidence of authenticity, and odd metadata is a probabilistic lead, not proof of manipulation. No pixel- or audio-level manipulation analysis.

name: Meedan Check
description: Self-hostable collaborative media annotation and fact-checking workflow platform. The meedan/check repo is the Docker development environment orchestrating component services (check-api content management, check-web UI, pender URL parsing/archiving, alegre similarity).
journalism_use_case: Newsroom and fact-checking desk workflow: ingest claims from tiplines and social monitoring, deduplicate against previously-checked claims, assign and track verification tasks across a team, publish fact-check outputs.
language_stack: Shell orchestration over Ruby/Rails, JavaScript/React, Python; Docker Compose
deployment: self-hosted via Docker Compose; also offered as Meedan-hosted SaaS
activity_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-16: 131 stars, last push 2026-09-23, archived=false. Components more active: check-api 2026-11-13, check-web 2026-11-11, pender 2026-11-16.
external_deps: Docker, PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Redis; optional Google Translate API; Sentry; Smooch/Sunshine Conversations for tiplines
data_flows: Self-hosting keeps content on your infrastructure. Optional integrations send data off-box: Google Translate API, Sentry telemetry, WhatsApp/Telegram tipline APIs. Hosted Check is governed by Meedan terms, not the MIT licence.
limitations: Multi-service stack with non-trivial ops burden; the dev-environment repo is not a production install. Similarity matching is a probabilistic ranked suggestion, not a determination that two claims are equivalent - human review required.

name: Noiseprint
maintainer: GRIP-UNINA, University Federico II of Naples
description: CNN that extracts a camera-model 'noiseprint' - a learned noise-residual fingerprint - from an image, usable for camera-model source identification and for spotting regions whose fingerprint is inconsistent with the rest of the image.
journalism_use_case: Testing whether a photo's noise fingerprint is consistent with the camera model it is claimed to come from, or whether part of the frame carries a different fingerprint from the rest (a splicing indicator independent of JPEG block artifacts).
licence: not verified as OSS - LICENSE.txt restricts use to informational and nonprofit purposes, copyright GRIP-UNINA
deployment: local scripts; pinned to a legacy TensorFlow 1.x stack
activity_evidence: Commit feed: 2026-03-27 'training code' is the newest commit, preceded by documentation commits 2023-01-12 and a dataset addition 2020-08-11; 20 commits total, 158 stars, 9 open issues and 7 open pull requests unmerged
external_deps: TensorFlow 1.2.1 (long-obsolete), author-provided weights
data_flows: Local inference; no third-party service documented
limitations: Not open source - non-profit/informational use only, so commercial newsroom use needs legal review. TensorFlow 1.2.1 pin makes installation painful; open PR backlog suggests limited maintenance. Noise-residual fingerprints are probabilistic indicators, NOT conclusive proof of manipulation, and are attenuated by resizing, strong recompression and denoising - precisely what social platforms apply. Reliable source attribution normally needs reference images from the candidate camera.

name: PhotoHolmes
description: Python library packaging published forgery-detection and manipulation-localisation methods behind a common interface, with dataset loaders and evaluation metrics so methods can be run and benchmarked consistently on the same image.
journalism_use_case: Lets an engineer embedded in a verification team run several published localisation methods over one image and compare heatmaps, rather than trusting a single model; also useful for honestly benchmarking how badly a method degrades on recompressed images newsrooms actually receive.
model_licence: varies per bundled method; README flags TruFor as restricted to non-profit use
language_stack: Python >= 3.10; PyTorch; optional Hugging Face transformers per method
deployment: local Python install (pip install -e .)
activity_evidence: Commit feed's most recent entries are 2025-02-03 (PR #9 merge, README fixes) and 2025-01-30 README proofread; only 16 commits on main, 53 stars - low-volume and possibly dormant since early 2025
external_deps: PyTorch, optional Hugging Face transformers, per-method pretrained weights downloaded separately
data_flows: Weights for some methods are fetched from third-party hosts (Hugging Face, authors' links); inference itself is local
limitations: Outputs are probabilistic localisation maps and scores from research models, NOT conclusive proof of manipulation. Apache-2.0 covers the harness only - individual methods carry their own, sometimes non-commercial, terms, so each enabled method must be checked. No GUI; requires Python skills and GPU for several methods. Activity appears stalled since Feb 2025.

name: PyExifTool
description: Python wrapper that drives a single long-lived ExifTool process via its -stay_open flag and pipes data in and out, making bulk metadata extraction far cheaper than spawning one process per file.
journalism_use_case: The practical way to metadata-profile a dump of thousands of images - clustering a leaked image set by camera body, software signature or capture-time gaps - inside a Python pipeline.
licence: GPL-3.0-or-later OR BSD (dual-licensed; user may choose)
language_stack: Python 3.6+; requires the ExifTool binary >= 12.15 installed separately
deployment: local Python library, published on PyPI
activity_evidence: Repository page shows 312 commits, 197 stars, 26 forks, with GitHub Actions test and lint workflows; not archived
external_deps: ExifTool binary installed separately
data_flows: Local only; no network calls documented
limitations: Inherits every interpretive caveat of ExifTool - metadata is editable and routinely stripped, so outputs support leads rather than conclusions and are not proof. A wrapper, not a forensic method, and version-coupled to the installed ExifTool binary.

name: PySceneDetect
description: Python/OpenCV tool and library that detects shot cuts and transitions in video, exports per-scene timestamps, saves representative frames, and can split the source file via ffmpeg or mkvmerge. Ships multiple detectors (ContentDetector, AdaptiveDetector, ThresholdDetector), a Python API and a published Docker image.
journalism_use_case: First step in video verification: fragment an unknown clip into shots and pull one keyframe per shot so each frame can be reverse-image-searched, geolocated or compared against earlier uploads - the InVID/WeVerify keyframes workflow, runnable locally on files too large or sensitive to upload.
deployment: local CLI / pip library / Docker (ghcr.io/breakthrough/pyscenedetect)
activity_evidence: Repo page shows release v0.7.3 dated 2026-11-08, 1,776 commits on main, 5.5k stars, 52 open issues; not archived
external_deps: ffmpeg or mkvmerge required for video splitting; OpenCV
data_flows: Fully local - no network calls or API keys in the documented workflow
limitations: Detects cuts, not manipulation: it produces no authenticity judgement and no proof of anything. Content-based detection is threshold-sensitive and can over- or under-segment on heavily compressed, low-light or fast-motion footage; gradual fades are harder than hard cuts. Frame counts/timestamps depend on the decoder, so re-check keyframe times before citing them.

name: SelfBlendedImages (SBI)
maintainer: Kaede Shiohara, Toshihiko Yamasaki, University of Tokyo
description: Official PyTorch implementation of the CVPR 2022 Oral 'Detecting Deepfakes with Self-Blended Images', which trains a detector on synthetically self-blended real faces rather than on specific generators. Pretrained EfficientNet-B4 weights for FF-raw and FF-c23 distributed via Google Drive.
journalism_use_case: A generator-agnostic face-manipulation detector worth running as one signal in an ensemble, since it was designed for the case journalists actually face - a fake made with a tool nobody has trained on.
model_licence: Custom research-only terms: authors state code and pretrained model are 'freely available for research purpose' and commercial use requires a separate licence agreement
deployment: self-hosted, GPU
activity_evidence: Repo page shows 12 commits, 277 stars, 24 open issues, and a 2026 changelog entry pointing to a newer CVPR 2026 audio-to-expression deepfake paper by the same authors; not archived
external_deps: Pretrained weights hosted on Google Drive; facial landmark detection and preprocessing pipeline
data_flows: Local inference; weight download from Google Drive
limitations: Probabilistic signal only - never conclusive proof of manipulation. The authors' own cross-dataset AUCs show the spread: roughly 93.8% on Celeb-DF and 97.9% on DFD but only about 73.0% on DFDC when trained on FF-raw. Reproduction is fragile: a Feb 2023 bug fix requires restarting from preprocessing. No OSS licence file confirmed and commercial use explicitly restricted.

name: ShadowFinder
description: Takes an object's height, its measured shadow length, and a date and time, and computes the set of places on Earth where that shadow geometry is possible, plotting the result as a band on a world map. Available as a Colab notebook, a Python library and a CLI.
journalism_use_case: Classic chronolocation/geolocation: given a photo with a visible shadow and a claimed timestamp, narrow the possible latitudes and longitudes - or run in reverse to test whether a claimed location and time are physically consistent with the shadow in frame.
deployment: Google Colab notebook, pip install shadowfinder, or CLI
activity_evidence: Commit feed: 2026-09-03 PyPI publish workflow fixes and Python version support updates (PRs #39-41, NumPy 2 support), 2026-02-13 minor version bump (#35) and a suncalc DatetimeIndex fix; 627 stars, 35 commits on main
external_deps: suncalc, timezone grid data; Google Colab if the notebook route is used
data_flows: The Python/CLI route runs entirely locally and takes measurements, not the image itself. The recommended Colab route executes on Google infrastructure - avoid it for sensitive material and run locally instead.
limitations: Output is a probabilistic band of candidate locations, not a point and not proof, and only as good as its inputs: object height and shadow length must be estimated from the image (often the dominant error source) and the date/time must be correct in the right timezone. A wrong or spoofed timestamp invalidates the result; flat-ground and vertical-object assumptions fail on slopes or leaning objects. README notes the CLI is slow because it regenerates the timezone grid each run.

name: Sherloq
description: Desktop GUI toolkit bundling classic image-forensics analyses: file digests and hex view, EXIF/metadata and thumbnail extraction, histograms and comparison viewers, gradient/wavelet/frequency views, colour-space and PCA projections, noise characterisation, JPEG quality estimation and double-compression checks, plus copy-move, splicing, resampling and median-filter detectors; recent work added PRNU camera-fingerprint generation and matching.
journalism_use_case: A single local workbench to triage a suspicious photo: pull metadata, look for ELA/noise/JPEG-ghost anomalies, test for copy-move or splicing, and build a documented list of anomalies to take to further reporting.
language_stack: Python 3.11, PySide2/Qt, OpenCV, Matplotlib; bundles ExifTool
deployment: local desktop install; runs offline on the analyst's machine
activity_evidence: Commit feed: 2026-07-16 merge of PR #128 adding PRNU camera-source identification, 2026-07-12 and 2026-07-05 PRNU fixes, 2026-05-25 bundled ExifTool bumped to 13.55; 174 commits on master, ~3.3k stars
external_deps: ExifTool binary, OpenCV, PySide2, Matplotlib
data_flows: No third-party service or API key documented for core tools; analysis runs locally, which matters for unpublished or source-sensitive images
limitations: The author frames it as an educational/research toolkit rather than a definitive forgery detector. Every panel output is a probabilistic signal requiring expert interpretation, NOT conclusive proof of manipulation; JPEG- and noise-based cues are weakened or destroyed by social-media recompression, resizing and screenshotting. PRNU matching needs a reference set of images from the candidate camera.

name: SunCalc
description: Small JavaScript library computing sun position (altitude and azimuth), sunlight phases (sunrise, sunset, dusk), moon position, moonrise/moonset and lunar phase for any coordinate and time. README reports typical sun-position error of roughly 0.08-0.09 degrees against timeanddate.com.
journalism_use_case: The primitive behind shadow and lighting verification: given a claimed location and timestamp, compute where the sun should have been and check whether shadow direction, length and light quality in the photo agree - a cheap, strong consistency test on claimed time and place.
deployment: client-side or local Node library; ports exist in other languages
activity_evidence: Commit feed: 2026-11-10 release 2.1.4 fixing getTimes hanging on NaN inputs (#193), 2026-11-08 release 2.1.3 fixing getTimes with utcOffset near local midnight (#192); 169 commits, 3.5k stars
external_deps: none
data_flows: Pure computation, no network calls; safe to run client-side on sensitive cases
limitations: It computes astronomy, not verification: it cannot tell you anything about the image, and a 'mismatch' is a probabilistic indication that may reflect a wrong coordinate, wrong timezone assumption, terrain or building occlusion, a non-vertical object, or lens distortion rather than a faked photo - never conclusive proof. Recent releases fixed real edge-case bugs around NaN inputs and UTC offsets, so pin a current version.

name: ThreatExchange (PDQ / TMK+PDQF / vPDQ and Hasher-Matcher-Actioner)
description: Meta's open trust-and-safety hashing and matching stack: PDQ photo hashing (256-bit signatures), TMK+PDQF video hashing (256KB signatures), the simplified vPDQ frame-similarity video hash, the python-threatexchange (pytx) library, and Hasher-Matcher-Actioner (HMA), a deployable hash-matching service, with a cloud-agnostic Docker successor 'Open Media Match' in development.
journalism_use_case: Industry-standard hashing for a collaborative or newsroom-scale image/video corpus: hash incoming media and match against a bank of previously verified or previously debunked content, including across organisations. TMK+PDQF in particular answers the most common 'deepfake' claim - old real footage relabelled.
licence: BSD-3-Clause (repository LICENSE; README notes pdq/cpp/CImg.h carries its own separate licence; tmk/LICENSE.txt is BSD-2-Clause)
deployment: libraries run locally; HMA is AWS-deployable, with a Docker-based cloud-agnostic successor in development
activity_evidence: Commit feed: 2026-11-09 pytx shared fake SignalExchangeAPI for tests (#2039) and DBMStore exchange_commit_fetch (#2038), 2026-11-04 HMA release 1.2.2 (#2035); 2,222 commits on main
external_deps: FFmpeg (4.1+ recommended) for video hashing; optional OpenMP and FAISS; optional signal-exchange APIs requiring credentials; AWS for current HMA deployment
data_flows: Hashing and local matching need no network. Connecting an exchange API sends/receives hashes with a third party under that provider's terms and requires API credentials.
limitations: These are near-duplicate matching tools, NOT manipulation or AI-generation detectors: a match is a probabilistic signal meaning 'substantially the same media as something in the bank' and says nothing about authenticity. Meta's own docs say TMK is not for matching short clips out of a longer video or substantially altered content. Not adversarially robust - crops, flips, overlays and re-encodes push hashes out of range - and false positives rise as thresholds loosen. Requires C++ build skills; running HMA is a real infrastructure commitment.

name: TruFor
maintainer: GRIP-UNINA, University Federico II of Naples
description: Transformer-based forensic framework (CVPR 2023) fusing a learned high-level RGB stream with a low-level noise-residual fingerprint to detect and localise image forgeries, including conventional edits and generated/inpainted content. Outputs a pixel-level localisation map, a whole-image integrity score, and a reliability map flagging regions where its own prediction is error-prone.
journalism_use_case: Second-opinion localisation on a single contested photo, with the reliability map used to discount areas where the model is unreliable - useful precisely because it tempers false alarms rather than producing a bare score.
licence: not verified as OSS - LICENSE.txt restricts use to informational and nonprofit purposes
deployment: local inference via provided Docker image; training code under TruFor_train_test
activity_evidence: README changelog records test code released 2023-06-28 and training code released 2025-03-05; repository not archived
external_deps: Docker, PyTorch; weights obtained per repository download instructions
data_flows: Inference is local inside Docker, so images need not leave the newsroom
limitations: Not open source: licence permits only informational and non-profit use - a legal problem for commercial newsrooms. Outputs are probabilistic forensic signals, NEVER conclusive proof of manipulation; the authors ship a reliability map because false alarms are expected. As with all residual/noise-based detectors, platform recompression and resizing attenuate the cues it relies on.

name: UniversalFakeDetect
maintainer: Utkarsh Ojha, Yuheng Li, Yong Jae Lee (WisconsinAIVision)
description: Reference code for 'Towards Universal Fake Image Detectors that Generalize Across Generative Models' (CVPR 2023): uses frozen CLIP features with a lightweight classifier/nearest-neighbour head instead of a bespoke CNN, evaluated across 19 generative models spanning GANs and diffusion models.
journalism_use_case: A baseline for teams testing whether any synthetic-image detector holds up on their own case material - valuable mainly as the honest yardstick for cross-generator generalisation claims.
model_licence: not separately stated; weights distributed by the authors under the repo terms
deployment: local scripts; requires GPU and a large (~72GB) evaluation dataset download
activity_evidence: Commit feed: README update 2026-08-19, LICENSE file created 2025-01-06, substantive code commits 2023-08-20/22; 18 commits, 381 stars - research snapshot rather than maintained software

The repo notes its released diffusion evaluation set is reduced to 1k real / 1k fake per domain versus 10k in the paper, so reproduced numbers differ from published ones. Trained on 2019-2023-era generators; nothing substantiates performance on 2025-2026 models, and detector accuracy in this literature collapses on unseen generators and recompressed social-media copies.

name: X-FACT

Labels harmonised across organisations with differing rating scales, introducing noise. Outputs are probabilistic, not proof.

name: x-ray
description: Python library and CLI that detects bad redactions in PDFs - cases where text was visually covered with a black box but the underlying characters remain extractable in the document.
journalism_use_case: Triaging FOIA releases, court filings and leaked document sets for failed redactions that reveal names, figures or passages the releasing body intended to withhold - a recurring source of scoops and a routine check before relying on a 'redacted' document.
deployment: local library / CLI (PyPI)
activity_evidence: gh api 2026-11-16: BSD-2-Clause, archived=false, last push 2026-10-15, 837 stars
external_deps: PDF parsing stack (pdfplumber/pdfminer lineage)
data_flows: Local processing; no third-party service, which matters for sensitive leaked documents
limitations: Detection is heuristic: outputs are probabilistic signals flagging candidate bad redactions, not conclusive proof, and both false positives and missed redactions occur. It finds text-layer failures only - it cannot recover text that was genuinely rasterised away, and it says nothing about whether a redaction was legally proper. Publishing recovered redacted content raises separate legal and ethical questions.

name: yt-dlp
description: Feature-rich command-line audio/video downloader supporting thousands of sites, with format selection, subtitle and metadata extraction, live-stream capture, post-processing via FFmpeg and extensive per-extractor options.
journalism_use_case: The workhorse for securing a copy of social video before deletion - pulling the highest available bitrate (crucial because compression destroys artefacts detectors rely on), plus uploader metadata, upload timestamps, subtitles and thumbnails, and capturing live streams as they air.

activity_evidence: Repo page shows 24,040 commits on master, 208k stars, 18.4k forks, and active nightly and master release channels; not archived

The repo notes PyInstaller-bundled executables incorporate GPLv3+ code, making those binaries GPLv3+ even though source is Unlicense. Downloading raises terms-of-service and sometimes copyright questions per platform, and the fetched file is not a chain-of-custody-grade record unless you hash and timestamp it yourself.

journalism_use_case: The standard first stop for confirming and timestamping a national or regional internet shutdown, because agreement across three unrelated signals is hard to explain away as a measurement artefact.

limitations: The LICENSE text read on both the CAIDA and InetIntel copies grants use for academic research and education without fee and directs other uses to contact the university - so despite public code this is source-available, not OSI open source, and a commercial newsroom redeploying it should get permission. name: M-Lab NDT server, ndt7 client and MSAK
description: M-Lab's open measurement stack: the ndt5/ndt7 server with Prometheus integration, reference Go client, and MSAK ('Measurements Swiss Army Knife') for multi-stream throughput and latency tests, all feeding M-Lab's openly published dataset.
journalism_use_case: Evidence for throttling and degradation stories - the slow-lane variant of a shutdown, where connectivity technically persists but collapses in throughput - and for long-run comparisons of network performance by ISP and region.
deployment: self-hosted server/client, plus M-Lab's global hosted measurement platform and public dataset
activity_evidence: GitHub API: m-lab/ndt-server pushed_at 2026-10-15, release v0.26.1 published 2026-10-15 and v0.26.0 on 2026-10-06, 137 stars, archived=false; m-lab/msak pushed_at 2026-11-14 (last release v0.4.7 on 2024-10-07), Apache-2.0, 32 stars; m-lab/ndt7-client-go pushed_at 2026-09-22, Apache-2.0, 55 stars.
platform_api_risk: Low on the code side; the hosted platform and its BigQuery dataset are a single-provider dependency, and historical test families (ndt5 vs ndt7) are not directly comparable.
external_deps: Go toolchain, Docker, Prometheus for metrics; M-Lab's server fleet and BigQuery dataset for the hosted data.
data_flows: Tests measure the client's own connection; M-Lab publishes results openly including truncated client IP and ASN, a documented privacy trade-off journalists should disclose when citing it.
limitations: This is performance measurement, not censorship detection - it will not tell you a site is blocked, only that a path is degraded, and attributing degradation to deliberate throttling needs corroboration. MSAK's last tagged release is from 2024.

name: NewsDiffs
maintainer: Eric Price, Greg Price, Jennifer 8. Lee and contributors (ecprice)
description: Django website and scraping framework, built at a 2012 Knight-Mozilla MIT hackathon, that tracked silent edits to online news articles using hand-written parser modules per publication and published the diffs at newsdiffs.org. Its README still specifies Python 2.6+.
journalism_use_case: The canonical prior art for stealth-edit tracking and a useful reference for how to structure per-site parsers and a public diff archive; not a tool to deploy today.

deployment: self-hosted Django site plus scraper cron (2012-era instructions)

LICENSE read 2026-11-16: MIT/Expat text with a note that some files carry their own licences.

limitations: Effectively abandoned (last default-branch commit 2018) on an end-of-life runtime; README notes you must be a programmer to add a parser for each new site; mixed per-file licensing means reuse needs file-by-file checking.

name: OONI backend (measurements API, collector, test helpers)
maintainer: Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) Foundation ETS
description: Consolidated repository for OONI's server-side infrastructure: the measurements API, the collector that receives probe submissions, bouncers and test helpers, plus sysadmin tooling, merged from the older ooni/api and ooni/pipeline repos.
journalism_use_case: Data teams query the OONI measurements API to pull structured blocking counts per country, ASN and URL over time for charts and trend reporting, instead of hand-collecting from the web UI.
deployment: self-hosted server stack; the canonical instance is OONI's own hosted API
activity_evidence: GitHub API: pushed_at 2026-11-13; 60 stars; archived=false; absorbs ooni/api, ooni/pipeline, ooni/sysadmin, collector, bouncers and test-helpers. The superseded ooni/api is archived=true (pushed_at 2023-03-16) and ooni/pipeline is dormant (pushed_at 2023-08-17). https://api.ooni.io/ returned HTTP 200 on 2026-11-16.
platform_api_risk: Journalists relying on the hosted api.ooni.io are dependent on OONI's funding and rate limits; endpoint shapes have changed across backend generations, so pinned queries can break.
external_deps: ClickHouse/PostgreSQL-class data stores and OONI's own measurement storage; the probe fleet as the data source.
